question: According to the Connecticut CDL manual, what effect can overloading have on a commercial motor vehicle's brakes?
choice_a: Brakes can fail when forced to work too hard, and stopping distance increases
choice_b: Brakes automatically adjust air pressure to compensate for the extra weight
choice_c: Overloading has no effect on braking, only on steering
choice_d: Overloading only affects trailer brakes, not tractor brakes
explanation: The manual states that overloading increases stopping distance and that brakes can fail when forced to work too hard; overloaded trucks also must go slowly on upgrades and may gain too much speed on downgrades.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

topic: Center of Gravity and Cargo Placement
question: To reduce the risk of rollover from a high center of gravity, how should cargo be loaded on a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: The heaviest parts of the cargo should be placed under the lightest parts, as low as possible
choice_b: The heaviest parts of the cargo should be placed on top for better visibility
choice_c: Cargo weight distribution does not affect the vehicle's center of gravity
choice_d: All cargo should be piled as high as possible to maximize trailer space
explanation: The manual states it is very important to distribute cargo so it is as low as possible, putting the heaviest parts of the cargo under the lightest parts, since a high center of gravity makes the vehicle more likely to tip over, especially in curves.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What problem can result from too much weight on a truck's steering axle?
choice_a: Hard steering, which can damage the steering axle and tires
choice_d: Automatic activation of the parking brake
explanation: The manual warns that too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What can happen if there is too little weight on a truck's driving axles?
choice_a: Poor traction, causing the drive wheels to spin easily
choice_c: The vehicle automatically shifts to a lower gear
choice_d: The parking brake will fail to release
explanation: Too little weight on the driving axles can cause poor traction, so the drive wheels may spin easily, and in bad weather the truck may not be able to keep going.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What can cause an underloaded steering axle that makes a vehicle too light to steer safely?
choice_a: Shifting weight too far to the rear of the vehicle
choice_b: Shifting weight too far to the front of the vehicle
explanation: The manual notes that under-loaded front axles, caused by shifting weight too far to the rear, can make the steering axle weight too light to steer the vehicle safely.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What is the purpose of bracing when securing cargo, as described in the manual?
choice_a: It goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment to prevent movement
choice_b: It is placed only under the cargo to allow it to slide freely during transport
choice_c: It replaces the need for any tie-downs on flatbed trailers
choice_d: It is required only for hanging meat loads
explanation: Bracing is used to prevent movement of cargo and goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment, while blocking is shaped to fit snugly against the cargo at the front, back, and/or sides.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What is the minimum tie-down requirement described in the Connecticut CDL manual, regardless of how small the cargo is?
choice_a: At least two tie-downs, with at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo
choice_b: Exactly one tie-down per piece of cargo, no matter its length
choice_c: At least four tie-downs per vehicle, regardless of cargo size
choice_d: One tie-down for every 50 feet of cargo
explanation: The manual states cargo should have at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Under the federal regulations described in the manual, the aggregate working load limit of a cargo securement system must be at least how much of the weight of the article(s) being secured?
choice_a: One-half times the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_b: Equal to the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_c: One-quarter times the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_d: Twice the weight of the article or group of articles
explanation: Federal regulations require the aggregate working load limit of any securement system used to secure an article or group of articles against movement to be at least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Which of the following is listed in the manual as proper tie-down equipment for securing cargo?
choice_a: Ropes, straps, chains, and tensioning devices such as winches or ratchets
choice_b: Duct tape and bungee cords only
choice_d: Rope alone, which is sufficient for all cargo types
explanation: The manual specifies that proper tie-down equipment must be used, including ropes, straps, chains, and tensioning devices such as winches, ratchets, and clinching components, attached to the vehicle correctly via hooks, bolts, rails, or rings.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: What is the purpose of a front-end header board ("headache rack") on a cargo vehicle?
choice_a: To protect the driver from cargo moving forward in a crash or emergency stop
choice_b: To provide a mounting point for the vehicle's CB radio antenna
choice_c: To cover cargo and protect it from weather
choice_d: To increase the vehicle's Gross Vehicle Weight Rating
explanation: Front-end header boards, also called headache racks, protect the driver from cargo in the event of a crash or emergency stop by blocking the forward movement of any cargo carried.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: According to the manual, what are the two basic reasons for covering cargo?
choice_a: To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
choice_b: To improve fuel economy and reduce engine noise
choice_c: To hide the cargo from view and reduce theft
choice_d: To reduce the vehicle's overall height and improve visibility
explanation: The manual lists two basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather, noting spill protection is a safety requirement in many states.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: While driving, why should a driver periodically check cargo covers in the mirrors?
choice_a: A flapping cover can tear loose, uncover the cargo, and block the driver's or another driver's view
choice_b: Cargo covers are only inspected before the trip, never while driving
choice_c: Checking covers while driving is required only in Connecticut, not other states
choice_d: Cargo covers must be removed every 10 miles of travel
explanation: The manual advises drivers to look at cargo covers in the mirrors from time to time while driving because a flapping cover can tear loose, uncovering the cargo and possibly blocking the driver's view or someone else's.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Since a driver cannot inspect the contents of a sealed load directly, what should the driver still check?
choice_a: That the vehicle does not exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
choice_b: The color of the container's seal
choice_c: Only the manufacturer's name on the container
choice_d: Nothing further needs to be checked once a load is sealed
explanation: The manual states that although you cannot inspect sealed loads, you should still check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Why do dry bulk tanks require special care when driving?
choice_a: They have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, requiring caution on curves and sharp turns
choice_b: They are always overweight and require a special transit permit
choice_c: They cannot legally be equipped with any tie-down devices
choice_d: They must never be driven above 25 mph regardless of road conditions
explanation: Dry bulk tanks require special care because they have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, so drivers must be extremely cautious going around curves and making sharp turns.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: Why is a hanging meat load (suspended beef, pork, or lamb) in a refrigerated truck considered an unstable load?
choice_a: It has a high center of gravity, requiring particular caution on sharp curves such as ramps
choice_b: It is lighter than dry freight, making the truck prone to being blown over by wind
choice_c: It may only legally be loaded on flatbed trailers without sides
choice_d: It requires no tie-downs at all because it is suspended from hooks
explanation: The manual explains that hanging meat can be a very unstable load with a high center of gravity, and it advises particular caution on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps, going slowly.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: When hauling livestock with less than a full load, what technique does the manual recommend to keep the load stable?
choice_a: Using false bulkheads to keep the livestock bunched together
choice_b: Filling empty trailer space with sandbags
choice_c: Removing all partitions to give the livestock maximum room to move
choice_d: Driving only at night when livestock are calmer
explanation: With less than a full load, the manual recommends using false bulkheads to keep livestock bunched together; even when bunched, livestock can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3

question: What may be required when transporting over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads?
choice_a: Special transit permits, and possibly special equipment such as "wide load" signs, flashing lights, flags, or a police/pilot escort
choice_b: No special requirements as long as the driver holds a standard Class A CDL
choice_c: A permanent reduction in the vehicle's Gross Vehicle Weight Rating
choice_d: Removal of all mirrors to reduce the vehicle's overall width
explanation: Oversized loads require special transit permits, driving is usually limited to certain times, and special equipment such as "wide load" signs, flashing lights, and flags may be necessary; such loads may also require a police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and flashing lights.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-3
